"Tilka" is in the nominative position by supposing an omitted subject, meaning: "these are those." It is also said: "Tiyka ayatu al-kitab al-hakim," with "tiyka" as a substitute for "tilka." This is the reading of the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i. Hamzah read "hudan wa rahmatun" with the nominative, and this has two possibilities: the first is that it is by supposing an omitted subject, since it is the first verse; the second is that it is the predicate of "tilka." "Al-Muhsin" is the one who worships Allah as if he sees Him, and if he does not see Him, then indeed He sees him. It was also said: they are the good-doers in religion, which is Islam. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾ [[See vol. 5 p. 399.]] [al-Nisa': 125], the verse.

(﴿Who establish the prayer﴾) is in the position of a description. It is permissible to read it in the nominative by way of a new sentence, meaning "they are those who," and in the accusative by supposing "I mean" (a'ni). The discussion of this verse and the one following it has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1 p. 162 onward, and vol. 6 p. 221.]] and elsewhere.

Concerning this there are five issues.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿And among mankind is one who purchases idle talk﴾. "Min" (from/among) is in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence. "Lahw al-hadith" (idle talk) means singing (ghina'), according to Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others. Al-Nahhas said: It is forbidden by the Book and the Sunnah. The implied construction is: "one who purchases something possessing idle talk" or "something of idle talk," as in ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning "ask the people of the town." Or the implied meaning is: since he only buys it and exaggerates its price, as though he bought it for its frivolity. [Note in the original edition: this is as it stands in all manuscripts of the source. In al-Nahhas's book the text reads: "or the implied meaning is: since he only buys it and exaggerates its price, as though he bought idle talk." Both phrasings are obscure, and the sentence is probably meant to read: "or the implied meaning is that, since he only buys it and exaggerates its price for the sake of its frivolity, it is as though he bought idle talk."]

I say: This is one of the three verses which the scholars cited as evidence for the reprehensibility of singing and the prohibition of it. The second verse is God's words, ﴿while you are scornful﴾ [al-Najm: 61]. Ibn 'Abbas said: It is singing in the Himyarite dialect, "usmudi lana," meaning "sing for us." The third verse is God's words, ﴿and incite whomever you can among them with your voice﴾ [al-Isra': 64]. Mujahid said: this means singing and flutes (mazamir). The discussion of this has already passed in the commentary on Surat Subhan [see vol. 10, p. 290].

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Abu Umamah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Do not sell female singers, nor buy them, nor teach them. There is no good in trade involving them, and their price is unlawful." It was concerning such matters that this verse was revealed: ﴿And among mankind is one who purchases idle talk to lead astray from the way of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a gharib (singular) hadith, which is only transmitted through al-Qasim from Abu Umamah. Al-Qasim is reliable, but 'Ali ibn Yazid is weak in hadith. This was said by Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Mujahid interpreted it in this way. Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi mentioned it from al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i.

I say: This is the highest of what has been said about this verse. Ibn Mas'ud swore by Allah, besides whom there is no god, three times that it is singing. Sa'id ibn Jubayr transmitted from Abu al-Sahba' al-Bakri, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud was asked about God's words, "And among mankind is one who purchases idle talk," and he said: "By Allah, besides whom there is no god, it is singing," repeating it three times. It is also reported from Ibn 'Umar that it is singing, and likewise said 'Ikrimah, Maymun ibn Mihran and Makhul. Shu'bah and Sufyan transmitted from al-Hakam and Hammad, from Ibrahim, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "Singing causes hypocrisy to grow in the heart." Mujahid said the same, and added: "The idle talk in the verse is listening to singing and to similar falsehood." al-Hasan said: "Idle talk is musical instruments (ma'azif) and singing." al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: "Singing is falsehood, and falsehood is in the Fire." Ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Malik about it, and he said: God said, ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32]. Is it truth?!

Al-Bukhari included in the chapter at the end of the Book of Seeking Permission (Kitab al-Isti'dhan) the heading: "Chapter: every idle thing that is falsehood, when it distracts from obedience to Allah, and whoever says to his companion, 'Come, let me gamble with you.'" His statement, "when it distracts from obedience to Allah," is derived from God's words, "to lead astray from the way of Allah."

Also from al-Hasan: it is disbelief and polytheism (shirk). Some people interpreted it as referring to the narratives with which the people of falsehood and frivolity amuse themselves.

It was said: The verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he bought the books of the non-Arabs, such as those of Rustam and Isfandiyar. He used to sit in Mecca, and when Quraysh said that Muhammad had said such-and-such, he laughed at it, and he would relate to them the stories of the kings of Persia, saying: "My narrative is better than the narrative of Muhammad." This was related by al-Farra', al-Kalbi and others.

It was also said: He used to buy female singers. Whenever he found a man who wanted to embrace Islam, he would take him to his singing-girl and say: "Feed him, give him drink, and sing for him," and he would say: "This is better than what Muhammad calls you to: prayer, fasting, and fighting before him." This report and the first one clearly concern buying.

A group said: The "purchase" in this verse is metaphorical, and the verse was revealed concerning the talk of Quraysh, their amusement at matters of Islam, and their immersion in falsehood. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abandoning what must be done and adopting these reprehensible things is a "purchase" of them, in the manner of God's words, ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]; they bought disbelief in exchange for faith, meaning they substituted it for faith and preferred it over it.

Mutarrif said: "Purchasing idle talk" means liking it. Qatadah said: Perhaps he does not spend money on it, but listening to it is his purchase.

I say: The first opinion is the most preferable of what has been said on this subject, because of the attributed (marfu') hadith concerning it and the statements of the Companions and the Successors concerning it.

Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi added to the hadith of Abu Umamah: "No man raises his voice with singing except that Allah sends upon him two devils, one on this shoulder and the other on that shoulder, and they keep striking him with their feet until he is the one who falls silent."

Al-Tirmidhi and others transmitted from the hadith of Anas and others, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Two sounds are cursed and wicked, and I forbid them: the sound of a mizmar (wind instrument) at times of pleasure and merriment, and the wailing of the devil at a calamity: slapping of cheeks and tearing of garments."

Ja'far ibn Muhammad transmitted from his father, from his grandfather, from 'Ali, peace be upon him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was sent to break the mazamir (wind instruments)." Abu Talib al-Ghaylani recorded it.

Ibn Bishran recorded from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent to demolish the mazamir and the drum."

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted from the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When my nation does fifteen things, calamities will befall it," and he mentioned among them: "when singing-girls and musical instruments are adopted." In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "and singing-girls and musical instruments appear."

Ibn al-Mubarak transmitted from Malik ibn Anas, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sits with a singing-girl and listens to her, molten lead (al-anuk) will be poured into his ears on the Day of Resurrection." [Al-anuk: lead.]

Asad ibn Musa transmitted from 'Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Salamah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: It has reached us that Allah, the Exalted, will say on the Day of Resurrection: "Where are My servants who used to keep themselves and their ears free from idle talk and the flutes of the devil? Let them dwell in the gardens of musk, and inform them that I have granted them My good pleasure." [In vol. ج and ش: "gardens of Paradise."]

Ibn Wahb transmitted from Malik, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, the same, and added after "musk": "Then He will say to the angels: Let them hear My praise, My gratitude and My commendation, and inform them that there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve."

This meaning has also been related as a marfu' report from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever listens to the sound of singing will not be permitted to hear the ruhaniyyun (spiritual beings)." It was asked: "And who are the ruhaniyyun, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The reciters of the people of Paradise." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah recorded it in Nawadir al-Usul. We have mentioned, in the book al-Tadhkirah along with its parallels: "Whoever drinks wine in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter, and whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter," and other such reports. All of these are sound in meaning, as we explained there.

From the narration of Makhul, from 'A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies while possessing a singing slave-girl, do not pray over him." On the basis of these reports and others, the scholars said that singing is unlawful.

**The second issue:** This refers to singing that is customary among those famous for it, which stirs souls and incites them to passion and amorous poetry, and to debauchery which stirs what is still and awakens what is hidden. This kind, when it is in poetry that involves love-verse about women, description of their beauty, mention of wine and forbidden things, is not disputed as unlawful, because it is frivolity and reprehensible singing by consensus. As for what is free of such things, a small amount of it is permitted at times of joy, such as at weddings and festivals, and when encouraging people to undertake arduous tasks, as was done at the digging of the trench and in the chanting of Anjasha and Salamah ibn al-Akwa'. [Anjasha was a black servant who drove the camels of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he had a fine voice in his chanting, so the camels quickened their pace with his song.]

As for what the Sufis have innovated today, namely constant indulgence in listening to songs with exciting instruments such as the shababat (the reed pipe, a later coinage), the tar (drum), the ma'azif and the strings, it is unlawful. Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the war drum, there is no harm in it, because it rouses souls and terrifies the enemy. There is some hesitation concerning the yara'ah (shepherd's pipe). The daff (frame drum) is permitted. [Al-Jawhari: They sometimes called the shepherd's reed on which he plays hay'arah and yara'ah. (What is between the brackets is missing from manuscripts ج and ش.)]

Al-Qushayri said: Drums were beaten before the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day he entered Medina, and Abu Bakr was about to rebuke them, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Leave them, O Abu Bakr, so that the Jews may know that our religion is expansive." They were beating and saying: "We are the daughters of Najjar; how wonderful is Muhammad as a neighbour!" It has also been said that the drum at marriage is like the daff, and likewise the instruments that publicize a marriage may be used for it, with speech that is good and free of obscenity.

The third issue: persisting in listening to singing (ghina') is frivolity (safah) by which testimony is rejected, but if it is not habitual, testimony is not rejected. Ishaq ibn Isa al-Tabba' reported: I asked Malik ibn Anas about the singing that the people of Madina permit, and he said: "Only the immoral ones among us do it." Abu al-Tayyib Tahir ibn Abd Allah al-Tabari reported: As for Malik ibn Anas, he forbade singing and listening to it, and he said: "If someone buys a slave-girl and finds her to be a singer, he has the right to return her for a defect." This was the position of all the people of Madina, except Ibrahim ibn Sa'd, from whom Zakariyya al-Saji reported that he did not see any harm in it. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: As for Malik, it is said of him that he was knowledgeable in this art, and his position was that it is forbidden. It is also reported from him that he said: "I learned this art when I was a young man. My mother said to me: 'My son! This art suits only one who has a handsome face, and you are not like that.' So I sought the religious sciences, I accompanied Rabi'a, and Allah brought good out of that." Abu al-Tayyib al-Tabari said: As for the position of Abu Hanifa, he disliked singing, and he considered the listening to singing to be among the sins, while permitting the drinking of nabidh. The same is the position of all the people of Kufa: Ibrahim, al-Sha'bi, Hammad, al-Thawri and others, with no disagreement among them on this. Likewise, no disagreement is known among the people of Basra regarding the disapproval of this and the prohibition of it, except what is reported from Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-Anbari, that he did not see any harm in it. He said: As for the position of al-Shafi'i, he said: "Singing is disliked, it resembles falsehood, and whoever engages in it excessively is a fool whose testimony is rejected." Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi cited from his imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal three narrations. He said: Our companions have mentioned from Abu Bakr al-Khallal and his companion Abd al-Aziz the permissibility of singing, but they were only referring to the ascetic poems (al-zuhdiyyat) that were in their time. He said: On this basis is to be understood what Ahmad did not disapprove of. This is supported by the fact that he was asked about a man who died leaving a son and a singing slave-girl, and the boy needed to sell her. He said: "She is to be sold as an untrained (sadhija) slave, not as a singer." It was said to him: "She is worth thirty thousand, and perhaps if she is sold untrained she would be worth twenty thousand?" He said: "She is not to be sold except as an untrained slave." Abu al-Faraj said: Ahmad only said this because this singing slave-girl does not sing ascetic poems, but rather exciting verses that stir up passion (ishq).

This is evidence that singing is prohibited, for if it were not prohibited, it would not be permissible to forfeit the wealth of an orphan. This is like the statement of Abu Talha to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have wine for orphans?" He said: "Pour it out (arriqha)." Had it been permissible to make it suitable for use, he would not have commanded wasting the property of orphans. Al-Tabari said: The scholars of the regions have agreed (ijma') on the disapproval of singing and the prohibition of it. Only Ibrahim ibn Sa'd and Ubayd Allah al-Anbari departed from the majority, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Keep to the great majority (al-sawad al-a'zam). Whoever separates from the community dies a death of ignorance (jahiliyya)." Abu al-Faraj said: Al-Qaffal from our companions said: The testimony of the singer and the dancer is not accepted. I say: Since it has been established that this matter is not permissible, then taking payment for it is also not permissible. Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr claimed a consensus (ijma') on the prohibition of payment for it. This has already been discussed in al-An'am at the words of Allah: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am: 59], and that is sufficient. [[Note: see vol. 7, p. 3.]]

The fourth issue: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: As for listening to singing-girls (al-qayna), it is permissible for a man to listen to the singing of his slave-girl, since nothing of it is forbidden to him, neither outwardly nor inwardly, so how can he be prevented from enjoying her voice? However, it is not permissible for women to be uncovered before men, nor to tear down the veils, nor to listen to obscene speech (al-rafath). If that leads to what is not lawful and not permitted, it is forbidden from its beginning and uprooted from its origin. Abu al-Tayyib al-Tabari said: As for listening to singing from a woman who is not a mahram, the companions of al-Shafi'i said it is not permissible, whether she is free or a slave. He said: Al-Shafi'i said: "The owner of the slave-girl, if he gathers people to listen to her, is a fool whose testimony is rejected," and then he made his statement stricter, saying: "Then she is a pimp's arrangement (diyatha)." Its owner was called a fool only because he invited people to falsehood, and whoever invites people to falsehood is a fool.

The fifth issue: The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿so that he may lead astray from the way of Allah﴾. The reading of the majority is with a dammah on the yaʼ (li-yudilla), meaning: so that he may lead others astray from the path of guidance, and whoever leads others astray has himself gone astray. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Abu Amr, Ruways and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatha on the yaʼ (li-yadilla), as an intransitive verb, meaning: so that he himself may go astray.

﴿And take it in mockery﴾: The reading of the people of Madina, Abu Amr and Asim is with a raf' (wa-yattakhidha-hu, nominative), as a conjunction to "who buys" (man yashtari), and it is also permissible that it be a new sentence (mustaʼnaf). Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-yattakhidha" with a nasb (accusative), as a conjunction to "li-yudilla". For both readings, it is not good to stop at His words "without knowledge," and the stop should be at His words "mockery." The pronoun in "yattakhidha-ha" refers to the signs (al-ayat). It is also permissible that it refers to the way, because the word "sabil" may be feminine or masculine.

﴿Those will have a humiliating punishment﴾: meaning a severe punishment that humiliates them. The poet said:

"And I surely turned in distress to the Christians, after the cross had suffered a humiliating torment."

[[This verse is by Jarir from a qasida in which he satirizes al-Akhtal, its opening being: "I became grieved when youth departed... I wish the nights had perished before that."]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 10–11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾. "Tarawnaha" (that you see) may be in the genitive position as an attributive adjective (na't) of "amad" (pillars). Thus it is possible that there are pillars, but they are not seen. It is also permissible that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to "al-samawat" (the heavens), and there are absolutely no pillars there. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: the better view is that it is a new independent clause (musta'naf), and there are no pillars there; this was said by Makki. And "bi-ghayri 'amad" (without pillars) is a complete phrase (al-tamam). The discussion of this verse has already passed in (surah) al-Ra'd [[See vol. 9, p. 279.]].

(And He cast into the earth firm mountains) i.e., immovable mountains.

(Lest it should sway) is in the accusative position, meaning: out of dislike that it should sway. The Kufans take it to mean "li-alla tamida" (so that it does not sway).

(And He scattered throughout it every kind of creature. And We send down water from the sky, and We cause to grow in it every noble pair) On the authority of Ibn Abbas: every good kind. Al-Sha'bi interpreted it as referring to people, because they are created from the earth. He said: whoever among them is destined for Paradise is the noble (karim), and whoever among them is destined for the Fire is the base (la'im). Others have interpreted that the semen-drop (nutfah) is created from dust, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [is a subject and predicate. "Al-khalq" here means "al-makhluq" (the created thing), i.e., this which I have mentioned, which you witness, is "khalq Allah," meaning the creation of Allah, i.e., He created it without any partner.

(Show me then) O assembly of polytheists, (what those besides Him have created) meaning the idols.

(Rather, the wrongdoers) i.e., the polytheists (are in clear error), i.e., manifest loss. "Ma" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence, and its predicate is "dha," and "dha" here means "alladhi" (which). "Khalq" governs an omitted pronoun (ha'), the estimated sense being: "Show me what (ayy shay') they created, those besides Him." The clause is in the accusative position with respect to "arunī" (show me). The pronoun with "khalq" may be retained, referring to "alladhina" (those), meaning: "Show me the things which those besides Him created." According to this view, one says: "Madha ta'allamta, anahwan am shi'ran?" (What have you learned, grammar or poetry?). It is also permissible that "ma" is in the accusative position governed by "arunī," and "dha" is redundant (za'id); according to this view one says: "Madha ta'allamta, anahwan am shi'ran?"

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 12:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾. "Hikmah" (wisdom) is the second object of the verb. "Luqman" is not declined (does not take tanwin) because it has an added alif and nun at its end, so it resembles the pattern fu'lan, whose feminine is fu'la. It is not declined when definite because this is a second cause of heaviness (for the two causes are proper name and this pattern). It is declined when indefinite because one of the two causes of heaviness has been removed. This was said by al-Nahhas.

He is Luqman ibn Ba'ura' ibn Nahur ibn Tarih, and Tarih is Azar, the father of Ibrahim. Thus did Muhammad ibn Ishaq trace his lineage. It was also said: he is Luqman ibn 'Anqa' ibn Sarun, and he was a Nubian from the people of Aylah, as mentioned by al-Suhayli. Wahb said: he was the son of the sister of Ayyub. Muqatil said: it was mentioned that he was the son of the maternal aunt of Ayyub.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he is Luqman ibn Ba'ura', the son of the sister of Ayyub or the son of his maternal aunt. It was said that he was among the descendants of Azar. He lived a thousand years, and Dawud (peace be upon him) met him and took knowledge from him. He used to give legal rulings (fatwa) before the mission of Dawud, and when Dawud was sent, he ceased giving rulings. He was asked about this, and he said: "Should I not be content, since I have been relieved of it?"

Al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: Luqman was black, one of the Sudanese of Egypt, with thick lips. Allah gave him wisdom and withheld prophethood from him. On this view, the majority of the people of interpretation hold that he was a walī (a righteous friend of God) and not a prophet. Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi held that he was a prophet, and on this view the "wisdom" would be prophethood.

The correct view is that he was a man of wisdom through the wisdom of Allah, the Exalted, which is correctness in beliefs, understanding of the religion, and reason [[In the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya: (... and action).]], a judge among the Children of Israel, black, with cracked feet, and with thick lips, i.e., large lips. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others.

It is narrated from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Luqman was not a prophet, but he was a servant who reflected much, with good certainty, who loved Allah, so Allah loved him. He bestowed wisdom upon him and gave him the choice of making him a khalifah who judges with truth. He said: 'My Lord, if You give me the choice, I accept well-being and leave off trial. And if You insist upon me, then I hear and obey, for You will surely protect me.'" This was mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Tha'labi added: The angels said to him, with a voice they could not be seen by: "Why, O Luqman?" He said: "Because the judge is in the most grievous and turbid of positions. The wronged come to him from every place. If he is helped, he is worthy to be saved, and if he errs, he errs on the road to Paradise. Whoever is humble in this world is better than whoever is honored in it. Whoever prefers this world over the Hereafter, this world will expel him and he will not attain the Hereafter." The angels marveled at the goodness of his speech. Then he slept a sleep, and he was given wisdom, and he awoke speaking it. Then Dawud was called after him and accepted it, meaning the khilafah, but he did not stipulate what Luqman had stipulated, so he fell into sin more than once, and Allah pardoned him each time. Luqman used to support him with his wisdom. Dawud said to him: "Blessed are you, O Luqman! You were given wisdom and turned away from trial, while Dawud was given the khilafah and was afflicted with trial and tribulation."

Qatadah said: Allah gave Luqman the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom over prophethood. Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him while he was sleeping and scattered wisdom upon him, so he woke up speaking it. He was asked: "How did you choose wisdom over prophethood when your Lord gave you the choice?" He said: "If He had sent prophethood to me as a binding command ['azīmah, i.e., the obligatory duties He imposed on His servants], I would have hoped for help from Him in it. But He gave me the choice, so I feared that I would be too weak for prophethood, and wisdom was more beloved to me."

Its craft has been disputed. It was said that he was a tailor, as said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and he said to a black man: "Do not grieve that you are black, for three of the best of people were black: Bilal, Mihja' the freedman of 'Umar, and Luqman." It was also said that he gathered firewood each day for his master, a bundle of wood. He said to a man who was looking at him: "If you see me as thick-lipped, then from between them comes soft speech, and if you see me as black, then my heart is white." It was said that he was a shepherd. A man who had known him before saw him and said to him: "Are you not the slave of the family of so-and-so?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What has brought you to what I see?" He said: "The decree of Allah, the fulfilment of trusts, truthfulness of speech, and leaving what does not concern me." This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Jabir.

Khalid al-Rab'i said: He was a carpenter. His master said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for me and bring me its two best morsels." He brought him the tongue and the heart. He said: "Was there nothing in it better than these two?" He was silent. Then he ordered him to slaughter another sheep and said: "Throw away its two most wicked morsels." He threw away the tongue and the heart. He said to him: "I ordered you to bring me the two best morsels and you brought me the tongue and the heart, and I ordered you to throw away the most wicked and you threw away the tongue and the heart?!" He said to him: "There is nothing better than them when they are good, and nothing more wicked than them when they are wicked."

I say: This meaning is traced to the Prophet ﷺ in more than one hadith. Among them is his saying ﷺ: "Verily, in the body there is a morsel; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart." Numerous sound and well-known reports have come concerning the tongue, among them his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever is protected by Allah from the evil of two things will enter Paradise: what is between his jaws [[al-lahyan: the walls of the mouth, the two bones in which the teeth are set from inside the mouth, which every creature with jaws has]] and his legs..." the hadith.

Luqman's wise sayings are many and transmitted, and this is one of them. It was said to him: "Who are the most evil of people?" He said: "The one who does not care if people see him doing wrong." I say: This also has a meaning traced to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "All my community will be pardoned except those who openly proclaim [their sins]. Among open proclamation is that a man does a deed at night, then in the morning, though Allah had covered it, he says: 'O so-and-so, I did such-and-such last night,' and he spent the night with his Lord concealing it, and in the morning he uncovers what Allah had concealed." Abu Hurayrah narrated it, and al-Bukhari recorded it.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: I read from the wisdom of Luqman more than ten thousand chapters.

It is narrated that he entered upon Dawud (peace be upon him) while he was weaving coats of mail, for Allah had made iron soft for him like clay. He wanted to ask him, but wisdom overtook him and he remained silent. When [Dawud] finished it, he put it on and said: "What a fine garment of war you are!" Luqman said: "Silence is wisdom, but few are those who practice it." Dawud said to him: "Truly, you are named rightly as a wise man."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That give thanks to Allah﴾. In this there are two interpretations. One is that "an" (that) is in the sense of "ay" (namely), explanatory, meaning: "We said to him, give thanks." The other view is that it is in a position of accusative case and the verb is within its relative clause, as Sibawayh related: "I wrote to him that stand up," though this construction is, in his view, far-fetched. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom so that he would give thanks to Allah." It was also said: that is, "that give thanks to Allah," and he gave thanks, so he became wise through his thanks to Us. Giving thanks to Allah is obeying Him in what He has commanded. Its reality, linguistically and in meaning, has already been discussed in al-Baqarah and elsewhere.

﴿And whoever gives thanks, he gives thanks only for himself﴾, i.e., whoever obeys Allah, the Exalted, works only for himself, because the benefit of the reward returns to him.

﴿And whoever disbelieves, [then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy]﴾, i.e., disbelieves the blessings and does not affirm the oneness of Allah. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need﴾ from the worship of His creatures, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ in the eyes of the creation, i.e., praised. Yahya ibn Sallam said: "Ghani" means free of need from His creation, and "Hamid" means praiseworthy in His acts.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while he was admonishing him﴾. Al-Suhayli said: The name of his son was Tharan, according to the view of al-Tabari and al-Qutabi. Al-Kalbi said: Mushkim. It was also said: An'am, related by al-Naqqash. Al-Qushayri mentioned that his son and his wife were both disbelievers, and he kept admonishing them until they both embraced Islam. I say: This is indicated by his saying: (Do not associate partners with Allah; indeed, association is a tremendous wrong). In Sahih Muslim and others, from Abdullah, who said: When the verse ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82] was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: Which of us does not wrong himself? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said to his son: (O my son, do not associate partners with Allah; indeed, association is a tremendous wrong)."

There is a difference of opinion regarding his saying: "Indeed, association is a tremendous wrong." It was said that it is from the words of Luqman. It was also said that it is a report from Allah, exalted is He, separate from the words of Luqman yet connected to it in emphasizing the meaning. This is supported by the transmitted hadith that when the verse ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82] was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became apprehensive and said: "Which of us has not wronged?" So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "Indeed, association is a tremendous wrong," and their apprehension was calmed. Apprehension is only calmed if it is a report from Allah, exalted is He, and apprehension may also be calmed by Allah mentioning it from a servant whom He described with wisdom and rectitude.

"Idh" (when) is in a position of accusative, meaning "remember" (udhkur). Al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: "Idh" is in an accusative position governed by "atayna" (We gave), and the meaning is: "And We certainly gave Luqman wisdom when he said..." Al-Nahhas said: I think this is an error, because in the sentence there is a waw that prevents this. He said: "Ya bunayya" with a kasra on the ya, because it indicates the omitted ya; and whoever pronounces it with a fatha does so because of the lightness of the fatha according to him. The discussion of this has already passed in "Hud" [in the original manuscripts: "Yusuf", which is a misprint; see vol. 9 p. 39]. His saying "ya bunayya" is not in the true sense of diminutive, although it is in its form; rather it is for the sake of tenderness, just as one says to a man: "ya akhi" (O my brother), and to a child: "huwa kuwayyis" (he is nice).

**Issue 1.** This section contains eight issues. The first concerns His saying, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents﴾. These two verses are a clear interjection within the admonition of Luqman. It has also been said that this is part of what Luqman enjoined on his son, which God reported about him. That is, Luqman said to his son: "Do not associate anything with God, and do not obey your parents in associating (others with Him), for God has enjoined concerning them obedience in what is not associating (others with Him) and disobedience to God, the Exalted." It has also been said: that is, "And when Luqman said to his son," and "We said to Luqman, concerning the wisdom We had given him," and "We enjoined upon man concerning his parents." That is, We said to him, "Give thanks to God," and We said to him, "And We enjoined upon man." It has also been said: "And when Luqman said to his son, 'Do not associate,' and We enjoined upon man concerning his parents, good treatment, and We commanded people with this, and Luqman commanded it to his son." Al-Qushayri mentioned these opinions. The correct view is that these two verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, as has already been mentioned in (the commentary on) "al-'Ankabut" [[See vol. 13, p. 328.]], and this is the view of a group of the exegetes.

The summary of this chapter is that obedience to the two parents is not to be observed in committing a major sin or in neglecting an obligation incumbent on each individual (fard 'ayn, an individual obligation, i.e. one that every person must perform personally). Obedience to them is obligatory in permissible matters. In abandoning acts of worship, what is recommended (nadb, a recommended act) is to be preferred, and this includes the collective obligation (fard kifaya, a communal obligation) of jihad. Responding to one's mother during prayer is also (recommended) even when it is possible to repeat the prayer; yet this is stronger than the merely recommended, but it is justified by fear of harm to her or something similar, which permits interrupting the prayer, so it is not stronger than the recommended. Al-Hasan differed with this distinction and said: "If his mother prevents him from attending the 'Isha' prayer out of compassion, he should not obey her."

**Issue 2.** Since God singled out the mother by mentioning the pregnancy and the mention of nursing, she has three degrees (of precedence) in this, while the father has one. This resembles the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when a man said to him, "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?" He said: "Your mother." He said, "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said, "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said, "Then who?" He said: "Your father." So he gave him a quarter of the (sum of) good companionship, as in this verse. All of this has already been discussed in (the commentary on) "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 239.]].

**Issue 3.** His saying, ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾, means: she carried him in her womb while she grows weaker every day, weakness upon weakness. It has also been said: a woman is weak by nature, and then pregnancy weakens her further.

Isa al-Thaqafi recited "wahnan 'ala wahn" with a fatha on the ha' in both places, and it is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr; they both have the same meaning. Qa'nab ibn Umm Sahib said:

"Is there for the blamers one who forbids them, so that he restrains them?
Indeed, the blamers have in them fatigue and weakness."

It is said: wahana, yahinu; wahuna, yawhunu, and wahina, yahinu, like warima, yarimu. "Wahnan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), as al-Qushayri mentioned. Al-Nahhas said: it is in the accusative as a second object with the preposition omitted, i.e. she carried him with weakness upon weakness.

The majority recited "wa-fisaluhu," and al-Hasan and Ya'qub recited "wa-fislahu." Both are (valid) dialectal forms, meaning that his weaning is within two years. The intended meaning of al-fisal is weaning (al-fitam), but it is expressed by its end and its limit. It is said: "infasala 'an kadha," meaning it separated and became distinct, and by this the young camel (fasil) was named.

**Issue 4.** The scholars agree on the two years as the period of nursing with regard to legal rulings and maintenance. As for the prohibition of milk kinship, one group limited it to a full year, with no increase or decrease. Another group said: two years, and what is connected to them of a month or similar, if the nursing is continuous. Another group said: if the child was weaned before the two years and left off milk, then what is drunk after that within the two years does not create prohibition. This has already been discussed fully in (the commentary on) "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 3, p. 160.]].

**Issue 5.** His saying, ﴿that give thanks to Me﴾: "an" is in the accusative place according to the view of al-Zajjaj, and the meaning is: "And We enjoined upon man concerning his parents, that give thanks to Me." Al-Nahhas said: and better than this is that "an" is explanatory (mufassira), and the meaning is: "We said to him, give thanks to Me and to your parents." It has been said: thanks to God is for the blessing of faith, and thanks to the parents is for the blessing of upbringing. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: whoever prays the five prayers has thanked God, the Exalted, and whoever supplicates for his parents after the prayers has thanked them.

**Issue 6.** His saying, ﴿But if they strive with you that you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, and keep them company in this world with kindness, and follow the way of those who turn back to Me. Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do﴾. We have already explained that this verse and the one before it were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas when he embraced Islam, and that his mother, Hamnah bint Abi Sufyan ibn Umayya, swore that she would not eat, as has been mentioned in the verse before it.

**Issue 7.** His saying, ﴿and keep them company in this world with kindness﴾: "ma'rufan" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e. "companionship that is kind." One says: "sahibtuhu musahabatan wa musahiban." "Ma'ruf" means what is good. The verse is evidence for maintaining relations with two disbelieving parents with whatever wealth is possible if they are poor, and for speaking gently and calling them to Islam with gentleness.

Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq said to the Prophet, peace be upon him, when her aunt, or it is said her foster mother, came to her: "O Messenger of God, my mother has come to me and she is desirous (of my favour). Should I maintain relations with her?" He said: "Yes." It has been said that "raghibah" means: averse to Islam. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The apparent meaning to me is that she was desirous of the relationship (of kinship), and she would not have come to Asma' had she not been in need." The mother of Asma' was Qutaylah bint 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Abd Asad. The mother of 'A'isha and 'Abd al-Rahman was Umm Ruman, who was early in Islam.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When Sa'd embraced Islam, his two brothers 'Amir and 'Uwaymir embraced Islam with him, and none of them remained a polytheist except 'Utba. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, threatened with the raising of those in the graves and their return to Him for recompense, and with reckoning for small deeds and great ones.

**Issue 1.** This section contains eight issues. The first concerns His saying, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents﴾. These two verses are a clear interjection within the admonition of Luqman. It has also been said that this is part of what Luqman enjoined on his son, which God reported about him. That is, Luqman said to his son: "Do not associate anything with God, and do not obey your parents in associating (others with Him), for God has enjoined concerning them obedience in what is not associating (others with Him) and disobedience to God, the Exalted." It has also been said: that is, "And when Luqman said to his son," and "We said to Luqman, concerning the wisdom We had given him," and "We enjoined upon man concerning his parents." That is, We said to him, "Give thanks to God," and We said to him, "And We enjoined upon man." It has also been said: "And when Luqman said to his son, 'Do not associate,' and We enjoined upon man concerning his parents, good treatment, and We commanded people with this, and Luqman commanded it to his son." Al-Qushayri mentioned these opinions. The correct view is that these two verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, as has already been mentioned in (the commentary on) "al-'Ankabut" [[See vol. 13, p. 328.]], and this is the view of a group of the exegetes.

The summary of this chapter is that obedience to the two parents is not to be observed in committing a major sin or in neglecting an obligation incumbent on each individual (fard 'ayn, an individual obligation, i.e. one that every person must perform personally). Obedience to them is obligatory in permissible matters. In abandoning acts of worship, what is recommended (nadb, a recommended act) is to be preferred, and this includes the collective obligation (fard kifaya, a communal obligation) of jihad. Responding to one's mother during prayer is also (recommended) even when it is possible to repeat the prayer; yet this is stronger than the merely recommended, but it is justified by fear of harm to her or something similar, which permits interrupting the prayer, so it is not stronger than the recommended. Al-Hasan differed with this distinction and said: "If his mother prevents him from attending the 'Isha' prayer out of compassion, he should not obey her."

**Issue 2.** Since God singled out the mother by mentioning the pregnancy and the mention of nursing, she has three degrees (of precedence) in this, while the father has one. This resembles the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when a man said to him, "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?" He said: "Your mother." He said, "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said, "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said, "Then who?" He said: "Your father." So he gave him a quarter of the (sum of) good companionship, as in this verse. All of this has already been discussed in (the commentary on) "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 239.]].

**Issue 3.** His saying, ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾, means: she carried him in her womb while she grows weaker every day, weakness upon weakness. It has also been said: a woman is weak by nature, and then pregnancy weakens her further.

Isa al-Thaqafi recited "wahnan 'ala wahn" with a fatha on the ha' in both places, and it is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr; they both have the same meaning. Qa'nab ibn Umm Sahib said:

"Is there for the blamers one who forbids them, so that he restrains them?
Indeed, the blamers have in them fatigue and weakness."

It is said: wahana, yahinu; wahuna, yawhunu, and wahina, yahinu, like warima, yarimu. "Wahnan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), as al-Qushayri mentioned. Al-Nahhas said: it is in the accusative as a second object with the preposition omitted, i.e. she carried him with weakness upon weakness.

The majority recited "wa-fisaluhu," and al-Hasan and Ya'qub recited "wa-fislahu." Both are (valid) dialectal forms, meaning that his weaning is within two years. The intended meaning of al-fisal is weaning (al-fitam), but it is expressed by its end and its limit. It is said: "infasala 'an kadha," meaning it separated and became distinct, and by this the young camel (fasil) was named.

**Issue 4.** The scholars agree on the two years as the period of nursing with regard to legal rulings and maintenance. As for the prohibition of milk kinship, one group limited it to a full year, with no increase or decrease. Another group said: two years, and what is connected to them of a month or similar, if the nursing is continuous. Another group said: if the child was weaned before the two years and left off milk, then what is drunk after that within the two years does not create prohibition. This has already been discussed fully in (the commentary on) "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 3, p. 160.]].

**Issue 5.** His saying, ﴿that give thanks to Me﴾: "an" is in the accusative place according to the view of al-Zajjaj, and the meaning is: "And We enjoined upon man concerning his parents, that give thanks to Me." Al-Nahhas said: and better than this is that "an" is explanatory (mufassira), and the meaning is: "We said to him, give thanks to Me and to your parents." It has been said: thanks to God is for the blessing of faith, and thanks to the parents is for the blessing of upbringing. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: whoever prays the five prayers has thanked God, the Exalted, and whoever supplicates for his parents after the prayers has thanked them.

**Issue 6.** His saying, ﴿But if they strive with you that you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, and keep them company in this world with kindness, and follow the way of those who turn back to Me. Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do﴾. **Issue 8.** His saying, ﴿and follow the way of those who turn back to Me﴾: this is an admonition to all the world, as if the one commanded is the human being. "Anaba" means he inclined and returned to a thing, and this is the way of the prophets and the righteous. Al-Naqqash related that the one commanded was Sa'd, and the one who turned back was Abu Bakr. He said: When Abu Bakr embraced Islam, Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, 'Uthman, Talhah, Sa'id, and al-Zubayr came to him and said, "You have believed!" He said, "Yes," so this was revealed concerning him: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord?﴾ [Al-Zumar: 9]. When the six heard it, they believed. So God, the Exalted, revealed concerning them: ﴿And those who avoid the evil ones, not worshipping them, and turn back to God, for them is good tidings﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 243 onward.]] — up to His saying — ﴿those are the ones whom God has guided﴾ [Al-Zumar: 17–18]. Ibn 'Abbas said: When Sa'd embraced Islam, his two brothers 'Amir and 'Uwaymir embraced Islam with him, and none of them remained a polytheist except 'Utba. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, threatened with the raising of those in the graves and their return to Him for recompense, and with reckoning for small deeds and great ones.

The meaning: Luqman said to his son, "O my little son." This statement of Luqman's was intended only to inform his son of the extent of God's power, and this is the limit of what he could make him understand. It is said that a mustard seed's weight is not perceived by the senses, since it does not tip a scale. The meaning is that even if a person had a provision equal in weight to a mustard seed, in these places God would bring it to him until it reached the one for whom it was provided. The point is that one should not be so preoccupied with provision that it occupies him from performing the obligations and from following the way of those who turn to Me. I say: the Prophet ﷺ said to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, "Do not burden yourself with worry over what is decreed to happen, and what you are destined to receive will come to you." This verse also states that God has encompassed everything in knowledge and has counted everything in number, glory be to Him, with no partner.

It is related that the son of Luqman asked his father about a grain that falls to the bottom of the sea, whether God knows of it. Luqman answered him with this verse. It has also been said that the meaning concerns deeds, both sins and acts of obedience. That is, if the good deed or the sin is of the weight of a grain, God will bring it forth, meaning that nothing will escape the person whose doing of it has been decreed. In this sense, the admonition contains both encouragement and warning, together with a demonstration of God's power. In the first interpretation, there is neither encouragement nor warning.

God's statement ﴿the weight of a grain﴾ is an expression that may apply to substances, meaning the amount of a grain, and it may apply to deeds, meaning that what is weighed in an equivalent manner is the amount of a grain. What supports the view of those who say it refers to substances is the reading of Abd al-Karim al-Jazari (in manuscript J: "al-Jawzi") "fatakun" with a kasra on the kaf and a shadda on the nun, from the root kinn, which means something covered. The majority of reciters read "in taku" with the taa at the beginning, and "mithqal" in the accusative as the predicate of kana (the predicate of kāna, the verb "to be"). Its subject is an implied pronoun, whose assumed reference is "your question," according to what has been related, or "the sin and the act of obedience" according to the second view. What supports the soundness of this second view is the statement of the son of Luqman to his father: "Father, if I commit a sin where no one sees me, how will God know of it?" Then Luqman said to him, "O my little son, indeed if it be the weight of a mustard seed, and it is in a rock," and the verse continues. The son kept trembling until he died, as related by Muqatil.

The pronoun in "innaha" (indeed it) is the pronoun of the story, as when you say, "Indeed she is Hind standing," meaning the matter is that it is, indeed, if it be the weight of a grain. The Basran grammarians permit "innaha Zaydun darabtuhu" (indeed it, Zayd, I struck him), in the sense of "indeed the matter." The Kufan grammarians permit this only with a feminine noun, as we have mentioned. Nafi' read "mithqal" with a damma, and on this reading "taku" refers back to the meaning of "khardala" (mustard seed), that is, "if it be a grain of mustard." It has also been said that the verb attached to "mithqal" carries the feminine marker because it is attached to a feminine noun of which it is a part, since the weight of a grain of mustard is either an evil deed or a good one, as in His statement ﴿for him is ten times the like of it﴾ [al-An'am: 160], where the feminine form is used although "mithl" (like) is masculine, because He intended the good deeds. This is like the verse of the poet:

They walked as spears sway, their tips made light and shaken by the gusts of the blowing winds.

Here "taku" means "to occur" or "to happen," and so it does not require a predicate.

God's statement ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾: It has been said that the meaning of the speech is exaggeration and thoroughness in making the point clear, that is, that His power reaches whatever is within the crevices of a rock and whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Ibn Abbas said: the rock is beneath the seven earths, and the earth rests upon it. It has also been said: it is the rock on the back of the fish. Al-Suddi said: it is a rock that is not in the heavens or the earth, but beyond the seven earths, upon which stands an angel. He says this because God said ﴿or in the heavens or in the earth﴾, and those two suffice without the phrase ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾. What he said is possible, and it may also be said that the phrase ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾ is an emphasis, like His statement ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance﴾ [al-Alaq: 1–2], and His statement ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 17:

There are three issues in this verse.

The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my son, establish the prayer﴾. He enjoined his son with the greatest of acts of obedience, which are the prayer and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. He intends this only after he has himself carried out that duty and restrained himself from wrongdoing, and these are all acts of obedience and virtues together. How well the one who said:

*Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error,*
*and when it refrains from it, then you are wise.*

(This is among verses whose mention has already passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 367.]].)

The second is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And bear patiently what befalls you﴾. It requires urging to change wrongdoing even if harm reaches you. It indicates that the one who changes wrongdoing is sometimes harmed. This degree is on the basis of recommendation (nadb) and strength in the cause of God, but not on the basis of obligation (luzum). The discussion of this has already been completed in "Al 'Imran" and "al-Ma'idah" [[See vol. 4, p. 47, and vol. 6, p. 243.]]. It has been said: He commanded him to be patient over the hardships of this world, such as illnesses and others, and not to pass from impatience into disobedience to God, mighty and majestic. This is a good view because it is general.

The third is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Patience in the face of what is disliked is among the realities of faith. It has been said: establishing the prayer, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are among the matters requiring determination, that is, among what God has resolved and commanded. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. It is also possible that he means that this is among the noble characteristics and the firm resolutions of people of prudence who travel the path of salvation. Ibn Jurayj's statement is more correct.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 31, verse 18:**

There are three issues concerning this verse.

The first: Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read *tusa'ir* (تُصَاعِرْ) with an *alif* after the *sad*. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan and Mujahid read *tusa'ir* (تُصَعِّرْ) with a doubled *'ayn*. al-Jahdari read *tus'ir* (تُصْعِرْ) with the *sad* vowelless. The meaning is close in all of these. *Al-sa'ar* (الصَّعَرُ) means inclination (to the side). From this is the saying of the Bedouin: "Time has kept my neck bent, after I had straightened its bend." From the same root is the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum al-Taghlibi:

"We, when the tyrant turned his cheek away (in arrogance), straightened him from his inclination, and he became upright."

[[He means: "so you became upright."]]

al-Tabari recited it as "fa-taqawwamā" (فَتَقَوَّمَا). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is an error, because the rhyme of the poem is in the genitive (مَخْفُوضَةٌ). [[Before this verse, as in Mu'jam al-Shu'ara' by al-Marzubani:

"We confront the kings with the truth whatever they intend against us, and it is not forbidden for us to kill them."

al-Marzubani said: this verse, the verse of evidence, is narrated from the qasidah of al-Mutallis, whose opening is:

"My mother's people reproach me, and you will never see a man of generosity except by being generous."]] In another verse:

"We straightened for him from his cheek, the one turned away."

al-Harawi said: *"lā tuṣā'ir"* means: do not turn away from them out of arrogance towards them. It is said: the camel has *sa'ar* and *sayad* when it is afflicted with a disease by which its neck is twisted. Then it is said of the arrogant man: "he has *sa'ar* and *sayad*." So the meaning of *"lā tusa''ir"* is: do not make your cheek bear the *sa'ar*. In a hadith: "There will come upon people a time when there will be none among them but the *asda'* or the *abtar*." The *asda'* is the one who turns his face away in pride, and he meant the scum of people who have no religion. In a hadith: "Every *sa''ar* is cursed," meaning every one of pomp and arrogance.

The second: the meaning of the verse is: do not incline your cheek to people out of arrogance over them, self-admiration, and contempt for them. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas and a group. It is also said: it is to twist your jaw when a man is mentioned in your presence, as though you despise him. So the meaning is: turn towards them humbly, friendly, seeking companionship, and when the youngest of them speaks to you, listen to him until he completes his speech. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) used to do.

I say: from this meaning is what Malik narrated from Ibn Shihab, from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not hate one another, do not turn your backs on one another, do not envy one another, and be servants of Allah as brothers. It is not lawful for a Muslim to forsake his brother for more than three days." So *al-tadabbur* (التَّدَابُرُ) is turning away, abandoning speech, greeting and the like. Turning away is called *tadabbur* because whomever you hate, you turn away from and present your back (*dubr*) to him, and he does the same to you. Whomever you love, you turn to with your face and face him, so that you may gladden him and he may gladden you. So the meaning of *tadabbur* is present in the one who turns his cheek away, and Mujahid explained the verse with this meaning.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: His saying, "and do not turn your cheek away from people," seems to forbid a person from humiliating himself without need. Similar to this, it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It is not for a person to humiliate himself."

The third: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَلا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحاً﴾ [And do not walk on the earth exultantly]. *Maran* (مَرَحاً) means strutting and arrogant, a verbal noun (مَصْدَرٌ) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (حَالٌ). It has been discussed under "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 260.]]. It is liveliness and walking with joy without occupation and without need. The people of this character are constantly given to boasting and self-conceit, so the *maraḥ* is one who is haughty in his walk. Yahya ibn Jabir al-Ta'i narrated from Ibn 'A'idh al-Azdi, from Ghudayf ibn al-Harith, who said: I came to Bayt al-Maqdis, I and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr [[This name appears garbled in the manuscripts of the original. The correction is from Tahdhib al-Tahdhib.]]. He said: We sat with 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, and I heard him say: "The grave speaks to the servant when he is placed in it, saying: O son of Adam, what deceived you about me? Did you not know that I am the house of loneliness? Did you not know that I am the house of darkness? Did you not know that I am the house of truth? O son of Adam, what deceived you about me? You used to walk around me *faddaran*." Ibn 'A'idh said: I said to Ghudayf: What is *al-faddad*, O Abu Asma'? He said: Like some of your walking, O nephew, at times. Abu 'Ubayd said: the meaning is one with much wealth and one with arrogance.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever drags his garment out of arrogance, Allah will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection."

Al-fakhur (الْفَخُورُ) is the one who enumerates what he has been given and does not thank Allah the Exalted. Mujahid said this. The word *fakhr* also includes boasting about lineage and other things.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 19:

There are six issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be moderate in your pace﴾. When He forbade him the blameworthy character, He laid out for him the praiseworthy character that he should adopt, so He said: "And be moderate in your pace," meaning, be balanced in it. Qasd (moderation) is what lies between hastening and slowness: that is, do not walk with the dragging gait of those who feign weakness, nor leap with the leaping of the rowdy (shuttar). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hastiness in walking takes away the radiance of the believer." As for what is narrated from him, peace be upon him, that when he walked he walked quickly, and the saying of Aisha concerning Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When he walked, he walked quickly," she meant a quickness that is elevated above the dragging gait of the feeble, and Allah knows best. Allah, glory be to Him, has praised whoever has this description, as has already been explained in "al-Furqan" [[See vol. 13, p. 68.]].

The second: His saying: ﴿And lower your voice﴾, meaning reduce it, that is, do not strain to raise the voice; take from it what you need, for shouting louder than necessary is an affected strain that causes harm. The purpose of all of this is humility. Umar said to a muezzin who strained to raise the call to prayer beyond his capacity: "I feared that your murayta would burst!" The muezzin was Abu Mahdhurah Samurah ibn Mi'yar [[In the originals: (Ma'mar) with a mim instead of a ya, which is a distortion.]]. The murayta is the area between the navel and the pubic region.

The third: His saying: ﴿Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾, meaning the ugliest and most dreadful of them. From this comes the expression "atana bi-wajhin munkar" (he came to us with a hateful face). The donkey is a proverbial image for severe blame and insult, and likewise its braying. Because of their extreme disdain for mentioning it plainly, they use euphemisms and avoid explicit naming, saying "the one with long ears," just as unpleasant things are referred to by euphemism. It is counted among the vices of manners for the donkey to be mentioned in the gathering of people of dignity. Some Arabs refuse to ride a donkey out of disdain, even if walking on foot becomes hard for them [[al-rajlah (with a dammah and then a sukun): walking on foot.]]. The Prayer and Peace be upon him used to ride it, out of humility and submission before Allah, blessed and exalted.

The fourth: In the verse there is evidence that the ugliness of raising the voice in address and in quarrelling [[al-mula'ahah: mutual reproach and hostility.]] is defined by the ugliness of the voices of donkeys, because they are loud. In the Sahih, it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "When you hear the braying of donkeys, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, for they have seen a devil." It has also been narrated that no donkey brays and no dog barks except that it sees a devil. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "The cry of every creature is glorification (tasbih) except the braying of donkeys." Ata said: "The braying of donkeys is a supplication against the oppressors."

The fifth: [[In K: (In this verse is a permission from Allah, exalted, to leave off raising the voice and shouting.)]] This verse is a discipline from Allah, exalted, to abandon shouting in people's faces with contempt for them, or to abandon shouting altogether. The Arabs used to take pride in loud, booming voices and other such things; whoever among them had the loudest voice was the most honoured, and whoever had the lowest was the most humiliated, until their poet said:

Loud of speech, loud of sneezing,
Loud of appearance, loud of camels.

And he runs with exhaustion in the manner of the ostrich's running,
And he overcomes men with a complete (perfect) make-up.

So Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, forbade these jahiliyyah traits by His saying: "Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys," meaning: if anything were feared for its voice, it would be the donkey, so He placed them equal in the comparison.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the voice of donkeys﴾. The lam is for emphasis. He used the singular "voice" though it is attached to a plural, because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and a masdar indicates multiplicity. It is the masdar of sa'at, yasuwtu, sawtan, so he is sa'it. It is also said: sawwata, tasweetan, so he is musawwit. And a man is sa't, meaning loud-voiced, in the sense of sa'it, like the saying of them: rijal mal and nal, meaning those of much wealth and much giving.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 31, verses 20–21:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that Allah has made subservient to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth?﴾ He mentioned His blessings upon the children of Adam, and that He made subservient to them "whatever is in the heavens," namely the sun, the moon, the stars, and the angels who guard them and bring to them their benefits. "And whatever is in the earth" is general, including the mountains, the trees, the fruits, and what cannot be counted.

﴿And He has lavished upon you His blessings﴾, meaning He completed and perfected them. Ibn Abbas and Yahya ibn Umara recited "wa-asbagha" with the *sad* (ص) in place of the *sin* (س), as a substitution (*ibdal*), because the letters of elevation (*huruf al-isti'la'*, the emphatic letters that raise the tongue) draw the *sin* from its lower position to its upper one, so it becomes a *sad*. The word "ni'am" is the plural of "ni'mah," like "sidrah" and "sidar" (with a *fatha* on the *dal*). This is the reading of Nafi', Abu Amr, and Hafs. The rest read "ni'mah" in the singular, and the singular indicates plurality, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you should count the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. [See vol. 9, p. 366 onward.] This is the reading of Ibn Abbas by way of sound transmissions.

It has also been said that its meaning is Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn Abbas, when he asked him about this verse: "The apparent is Islam and the good of your character, and the hidden is what has been concealed from you of your evil deeds."

Al-Nahhas said: The explanation of this is that Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But He wishes to purify you and to complete His blessing upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], that He said: He will admit you to Paradise. The completion of Allah's blessing upon the servant is that He admits him to Paradise; likewise, when Islam's outcome leads to Paradise, it is called a blessing.

It has also been said: the apparent is health and perfection of form, and the hidden is knowledge and intellect. Al-Muhasibi said: the apparent are the blessings of this world, and the hidden are the blessings of the Hereafter. It has also been said: the apparent is what is seen by the eyes, such as wealth, rank, and beauty among people, and the granting of success in acts of obedience; and the hidden is what a person finds within himself of knowledge of Allah, good certainty, and what Allah, the Exalted, repels from the servant of calamities. Al-Mawardi recounted nine sayings on this, all of which return to these.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge﴾. Its meaning has already been mentioned in (*al-Hajj*) [See vol. 12, pp. 5 and 15] and elsewhere. It was revealed concerning a Jew who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, inform me about your Lord, what is He made of?" Then a thunderbolt came and seized him. This was said by Mujahid, and it has already passed in (*al-Ra'd*). [See vol. 6, p. 298.] It has also been said that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to say that the angels are the daughters of Allah. This was said by Ibn Abbas. "Yujadilu" means he disputes, argues. ﴿Without knowledge﴾, meaning without proof, ﴿nor guidance nor an illuminating Book﴾, meaning a luminous, clear one, except the Satan in what he inspires into them. ﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. [See vol. 7, p. 77.] And except the blind imitation of predecessors, as in the verse that follows.

(﴿Even if Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾) They would follow him.

The Qur'anic text: "And whoever submits his face to Allah" (﴾, 31:22), meaning he sincerely devotes his worship and intention to Allah, the Exalted.

Its parallel is the verse: "And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer" [Ta-Ha: 112]. [See vol. 11, p. 248 ff.] In the hadith of Jibril, he said: "Tell me about ihsan." He said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."

"Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold" (فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقى). Ibn Abbas said: "It is 'There is no god but Allah.'" This has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah." [See vol. 3, p. 279.]

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Sulami, and Abdullah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar recited: "wa-man yuslim" (وَمَنْ يُسْلِمْ) with the form of aslama.

Al-Nahhas said: "Yuslim" (يُسْلِمُ) is more well-known in this context, as the Exalted said: "So say: I have submitted my face to Allah" [Al 'Imran: 20]. The meaning of "aslamtu wajhiya li-Allah" is: I directed my worship to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Yusallim" (يُسَلِّمُ) would be in the intensive form, but what is commonly used with sallamtu is that it means "I paid/handed over" (dafa'tu), as one says "sallamtu fi al-hintah" (I paid in advance for the wheat), and it may also be said "aslamtu."

Al-Zamakhshari said: Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "wa-man yusallim" with the doubled letter (tashdid), as one says: "aslim amrak" and "sallim amrak ila Allah" (entrust your affair to Allah). If you ask: why is it construed with "ila" when it is construed with "li" (lam) in the Exalted's words: "Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah" [Al-Baqarah: 112]? I say: its meaning with "li" is that he made his face, which is his very self and essence, sound (salim) for Allah, that is, pure for Him. Its meaning with "ila" goes back to the sense that he handed over himself to Him, just as goods are handed over to a man when they are delivered to him. What is intended is reliance upon Him and committing one's affairs to Him.

"And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs" (وَإِلَى اللَّهِ عاقِبَةُ الْأُمُورِ), that is, their final destination (maṣīr).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you. To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did.﴾ That is, We will recompense them.

(Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.)

(We will let them enjoy themselves briefly.) That is, We will keep them in this world for a brief period in which they enjoy themselves.

(Then We will force them.) That is, We will compel them and drive them.

(To a severe punishment.) This is the punishment of Jahannam (Hellfire). The word "man" (whoever) is applicable to the singular and the plural; therefore He said "kufruhu" (his disbelief), then He said "marji'uhum" (their return), and what follows it is according to the meaning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 25–26:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ That is, they acknowledge that Allah is their Creator, so why do they worship other than Him?

(Say: "All praise is for Allah.") That is, for guiding us to His religion; praise belongs to no one else.

(But most of them do not know.) That is, they do not reflect and do not contemplate.

(To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.) That is, ownership and creation.

(Indeed, Allah is the Free of need.) That is, free of need from His creation and from their worship; He only commanded them so that it would benefit them.

(The Praiseworthy.) That is, praised for His handiwork.
