Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 27:

When He argued against the polytheists with what He argued, He made clear that the meanings of His speech, glory be to Him, do not run out, and that they have no end. Al-Qaffal said: When He mentioned that He subjected to them what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that He showered them with blessings, He drew attention to the fact that if the trees were pens and the seas were ink, with which the wondrous works of God's creation, which indicate His power and His oneness, were written, those wonders would not run out. Al-Qushayri said: He referred the meaning of those words (kalimat) to the things that are within His power (al-maqdurat), and it is better to understand the verse as referring to the eternal speech (al-kalam al-qadim). Whatever is created must have an end, so when endlessness is denied of His power-objects, this is a denial of endlessness of what is capable of being brought into existence in the future; but what existence has encompassed and counted must necessarily be finite, whereas the Eternal has no end in reality. The discussion of the meaning of "the words of God" has already passed at the end of al-Kahf [[See vol. 11, p. 68.]]. Abu 'Ali said: By "the words," and God knows best, is meant what is within the realm of what can be decreed (al-maqdur), not what has passed from it into existence. This is similar to what al-Qaffal said, and the purpose is only to inform of the abundance of the meanings of God's words, which are in themselves infinite; the matter has been brought closer to human understanding through what has an end, because that is the greatest abundance humans know, not that they would run out with more than these pens and seas. The occasion of revelation of the verse indicates that the intended "words" is the eternal speech. Ibn 'Abbas said: The cause of this verse is that the Jews said: "O Muhammad, how are we addressed by this statement: *And you have been given of knowledge only a little* [[See vol. 10, p. 324.]] [al-Isra': 85], while we have been given the Torah, in which is the speech of God and His rulings, and you claim that it is an explanation of everything?" The Messenger of God ﷺ said to them: "The Torah is little out of much," and this verse was revealed; and the verse is Medinan. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: It has become clear that "the words" here refers to knowledge and the realities of things, because He, mighty and majestic, knew before He created creation what He would create in the heavens and the earth of every thing, and He knew what is in it of the weights of atoms, and He knew all kinds and what is in them of every hair and limb, and what is in the tree of every leaf, and what is in them of kinds of creation, and of the varieties of taste and color that they undergo. So if He were to name every creature individually, and name its parts according to what He knew of their few and many, and the states it passes through, and what increases in it at every time, and explain every tree individually and what branches it sends forth, and the measure of what withers of that at every time, then the explanation of each one of them would be written with what God, majestic is His praise, encompasses of it; then the sea would be ink for that explanation which God, blessed and exalted, explained concerning those things, and seven seas after it were to supply it, the explanation of those things would be greater still. I say: This is the meaning of al-Qaffal's statement, and it is a good opinion, God willing. Some people said: The Quraysh said, "This speech of Muhammad will be completed and will come to an end," so this verse was revealed. Al-Suddi said: The Quraysh said, "How much Muhammad's speech is!" So this verse was revealed.

His statement, exalted is He: *"And the sea, with seven more seas to supply it with ink"*. The reading of the majority is with the nominative (*al-bahru*) on the basis of the subject-predicate construction, its predicate being in the clause that follows, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as if he said: "and the sea is in this state." Sibawayh estimated it thus. Some grammarians said: It is coordinated with *anna* (*anna*), because it is in the position of nominative by way of the subject. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *"wal-bahra"* with the accusative, coordinated with *ma* (*ma*), which is the noun of *anna*. It was said: meaning "and even if the sea supplies it," that is, adds to it. Ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan read *yamudduhu*, from *amadda*. One group said: The two have the same meaning. Another group said: *madda* means the thing supplies part of another, as you say: "The Nile extended the canal (madda al-Nil al-khalij)," meaning it added to it; and *amadda* means the thing supplies what is not part of it. This has passed in *al-Baqarah* and *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 1, p. 209, and vol. 4, p. 194 onward.]]. Ja'far ibn Muhammad read: *"wal-bahru midaduhu"*. *"Mā nafidat kalimatu Allah"* has passed [[See vol. 11, p. 68.]].

*(Inna Allaha 'Azizun Hakim)* has also passed [[See vol. 2, p. 131.]]. Abu 'Ubayda said: The sea here means the sweet water that grows the reeds (al-aqlam), but salt water does not grow reeds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾. Al-Dahhak said: The meaning is that the initial creation of all of you is only like the creation of a single soul, and your resurrection on the Day of Resurrection is only like the resurrection of a single soul. Al-Nahhas said: The grammarians have also interpreted it this way, meaning "only like the creation of a single soul," as in: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82] [[See vol. 9, p. 245 and following.]]. Mujahid said: Because He says to the few and the many, "Be," and it is. The verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Asadayn [[Thus in the copies of the original. The Ruh al-Ma'ani has: (Abu al-Aswad).]], and Munabbih and Nubayh, the two sons of al-Hajjaj ibn al-Sabbaq. They said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, created us in stages: a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones. Then you say we will be resurrected as a new creation, all together in a single hour!" So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul," because Allah, exalted is He, is not burdened by what burdens the servants, and His creation of the whole world is like His creation of a single soul.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what they say, ﴿All-Seeing﴾ of what they do.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 29–30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not see that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night?﴾ It has been discussed in (Surat al-Hajj) and (Surat Al 'Imran) [[In the original: (al-Hajj and al-An'am), which is an error. See vol. 12 p. 90 and vol. 4 p. 56.]].

(And He has subjected the sun and the moon) meaning He made them subservient through their rising and setting, determining the terms and completing the benefits.

(Each runs to a specified term) Al-Hasan said: "until the Day of Resurrection." Qatadah said: "until its time, in its rising and setting, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it."

(And that Allah is Acquainted with what you do) meaning: whoever has power over these things must necessarily have knowledge of them, and whoever has knowledge of them has knowledge of your deeds. The reading of the majority is "taʿmalūna" with the (ta) as direct address. As-Sulami, Nasr ibn ʿAsim and ad-Duri from Abu ʿAmr read it with the (ya), as a report.

(That) meaning: Allah, exalted is He, did that so that you would know and acknowledge "that Allah is the Truth, and that what they invoke besides Him is the falsehood," that is, Satan, as Mujahid said. It was also said: it refers to the idols and images that they associated with Allah, exalted is He.

(And that Allah is the Most High, the Most Great) "Al-ʿAliyy" in His station, "al-Kabir" in His dominion.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 31:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that the ships﴾ — i.e., the ships (al-sufun) — "run" is in the position of the predicate. "On the sea by the favour of Allah" — i.e., by His kindness to you and His mercy to you in delivering you from it. Ibn Hurmuz recited "bi-ni'mati Allah" (by the favours of Allah), the plural of ni'mah (favour), which is the sound plural (jam' al-salamah); the original form had a moved ʿayn, but it was made sukun (vowelless). ﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾ — "min" (of) here is partitive (li-l-tab'id), i.e., that He may show you the running of the ships; this was said by Yahya ibn Salam. Ibn Shajarah said: "min ayatihi" means what you witness of the power of Allah Exalted in it. Al-Naqqash said: it means what Allah provides for them from it. Al-Hasan said: the key to the seas is the ships, the key to the earth is the roads, and the key to the sky is supplication.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one⦆ — i.e., steadfast in accepting His decree, grateful for His favours. The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He meant every believer characterised by this quality, because patience and gratitude are among the best traits of faith. The word "ayah" means sign, and a sign does not become evident in the heart of every believer; it becomes evident only to one who is patient in affliction and grateful in ease. Al-Sha'bi said: Patience is half of faith, gratitude is half of faith, and certainty is all of faith. Have you not considered His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one," and His saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for the certain⦆ [al-Dhariyat: 20].[[See vol. 17, p. 39.]] And he (peace be upon him) said: "Faith is of two halves: half patience and half gratitude."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 32:

Allah's words: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shade-canopies﴾. Muqatil said: "like mountains." Al-Kalbi said: "like clouds," and Qatadah said the same. It is the plural of ẓullah (canopy, shade), and the wave is compared to them for its immensity and height. Al-Nabighah said, describing a sea:

"It runs alongside them, green and shadowed, / and at its edges are the splitting of the jars."

The wave is compared to ẓilal (shades), which is a plural, although the wave is singular, because the waves come one after another and ride over one another like canopies. It was also said: the word carries the sense of the plural, and it was not pluralized because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its root is from movement and crowding, and from it comes "māja al-baḥr" (the sea surged) and "al-nās yamūjūn" (the people surge). Ka'b said:

"We came upon a wave of the sea, in its midst / ḥabābīsh (mixed tribes), some of them bareheaded and some helmeted."

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah recited: "mawjun ka-al-ẓilāl," the plural of ẓill.

﴿Calling upon Allah, making their religion sincerely His﴾: affirming His oneness, not calling upon anyone other than Him for their deliverance. This has already been discussed [[see vol. 8, p. 325.]].

﴿But when He brings them safely to land﴾: meaning, from the sea.

﴿Some of them are moderate (muqtaṣid)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: fulfilling what they pledged to Allah at sea. Al-Naqqash said: meaning he was just in the covenant, and he was faithful on land to what he had pledged to Allah at sea. Al-Hasan said: "muqtaṣid" is a believer who holds firmly to monotheism and obedience. Mujahid said: "muqtaṣid" is moderate in speech, concealing disbelief. It was also said: there is an ellipsis in the statement, and the meaning is: "some of them are moderate, and some of them are disbelievers." What indicates the omitted part is His words: ﴿And none deny Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾. Khattar means treacherous, and khatr means the worst treachery. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"Indeed, if you had seen Abu 'Umayr, / you would have filled your hands with treachery and perfidy."

Al-A'sha said:

"His dwelling is at al-Ablaq al-Fard of Taymaʾ, / a sturdy fortress, and a neighbor who is not treacherous."

Al-Jawhari said: al-khatr is treachery; one says "khatarahu," so he is khattar. Al-Mawardi said: this is the view of the majority. 'Atiyyah said: it means the one who denies. It is said: "khatara yakhturu and yakhtiru" (with dammah and kasrah) "khatran," as mentioned by al-Qushayri. Denying the signs means rejecting their very existence, while denying their evidences means rejecting what they demonstrate.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: "O mankind, fear your Lord" (يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اتَّقُوا رَبَّكُمْ). It means the disbeliever and the believer alike; that is, fear Him and affirm His oneness.

"And fear a Day when no father will avail anything for his son, nor will a son avail anything for his father" (وَاخْشَوْا يَوْماً لَا يَجْزِي والِدٌ عَنْ وَلَدِهِ وَلا مَوْلُودٌ هُوَ جازٍ عَنْ والِدِهِ شَيْئاً). The meaning of "yajzi" (يَجْزِي, to avail or to suffice) has already been discussed in al-Baqarah and elsewhere [see vol. 1, p. 377]. If it is said: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever has three children die before reaching puberty (al-hinth, i.e., the age of men when the pen records their deeds and sin is recorded against them), the Fire will not touch him except for the fulfilment of the oath (tahillat al-qasam)." And he said, "Whoever is tested with anything of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a barrier for him from the Fire." It is said in reply: what is meant by this verse is that a father does not bear the sin of his child, nor a child the sin of his father, and neither is held to account for the other. What is meant by the reports is that the reward of patience at the death (of children) and of kindness to daughters shields the servant from the Fire, and the child will precede him to Paradise.

"Indeed, the promise of Allah is true" (إِنَّ وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ), that is, the Resurrection. "So let not the worldly life deceive you" (فَلا تَغُرَّنَّكُمُ الْحَياةُ الدُّنْيا), that is, let it not delude you with its adornments and what it calls you to, so that you rely upon it, incline towards it, and abandon work for the Hereafter. "And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah" (وَلا يَغُرَّنَّكُمْ بِاللَّهِ الْغَرُورُ). The common reading here, in surah al-Mala'ikah (see p. 322 of this part) and in al-Hadid (see vol. 17, p. 247), is with a fatha on the ghayn (الْغَرُورُ, al-Gharur), and it is Satan according to Mujahid and others, who deludes creation, promises them the world, and diverts them from the Hereafter. In surah al-Nisa' (see vol. 5, p. 395): "He promises them and arouses their desires." Simak ibn Harb, Abu Haywah and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read it with a damma on the ghayn (al-Ghurur), meaning "do not be deceived," as if it were a verbal noun of gharra, yaghurru, ghururan. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is that one acts in disobedience while wishing for forgiveness.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 31, verse 34:

Al-Farra' claimed that this carries the meaning of negation, i.e., no one knows it except Allah, exalted is He. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: The meaning of negation and affirmation in it arises only from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ having specified this, for he ﷺ said concerning the words of Allah, mighty and majestic, ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but Him﴾ [al-An'am: 59]: ("They are these"). I say: We have mentioned in Surat al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 1 onwards.]] the hadith of Ibn Umar on this, which al-Bukhari narrated. And in the hadith of Jibril, peace be upon him, he said: ("Tell me about the Hour?" Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:) "The one asked about it is no more knowledgeable than the one asking. There are five which none knows except Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs, and no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾." He said: ("You have spoken truly."). This is the wording of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "Your Prophet ﷺ was given everything except five: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾," to the end of the verse. Ibn Abbas said: These five none knows except Allah, the Exalted, and no angel brought near nor prophet sent knows them. Whoever claims that he knows any of these has disbelieved in the Qur'an, for he has contradicted it. Then, the prophets know much of the unseen by Allah's informing them. The intent is to refute the notion of soothsayers, astrologers, and those who seek rain by the anwa' [[Al-anwa' is the plural of nawʾ, which is the setting of a star in the mansions at dawn in the west together with the rising of another opposite it at the same moment. The Arabs used to attribute rains, winds, heat, and cold to the one that set.]], and it may be known through long experience some things about the sex of the unborn child and other matters, as mentioned earlier in al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 2 onwards.]]. The experience may differ, the habit may be broken, and knowledge remains with Allah alone. It is related that a Jew who used to calculate the reckoning of the stars said to Ibn Abbas: "If you wish, I will inform you of your son's star, that he will die after ten days, and that you will not die until you go blind, and that I will not complete a year before I die." He said: "Where will your death be, O Jew?" He said: "I do not know." Ibn Abbas said: "Allah has spoken truly: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾." Ibn Abbas returned and found his son feverish, and he died after ten days. The Jew died before the year was out, and Ibn Abbas died blind. Ali ibn al-Husayn, the narrator of this hadith, said: "This is the most astonishing of hadiths." Muqatil said: This verse was revealed concerning a man from the people of the desert named al-Warith ibn Amr ibn Harithah, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "My wife is pregnant, so tell me what she will bear. Our land is barren, so tell me when the rain will fall. I know when I was born, so tell me when I will die. I know what I did today, so tell me what I will do tomorrow. And tell me when the Hour will come." So Allah revealed this verse. Al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi mentioned it. Abu al-Malih narrated from Abu Izzah al-Hudhali who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: ("When Allah wills to take the soul of a servant in a land, He makes for him a need in it, and he does not stop until he reaches it." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: "Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour," until his words "in what land it will die.") (Al-Mawardi mentioned it, and Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud with a similar meaning. We have mentioned it fully in the book al-Tadhkirah.) The common reading is "wa-yunazzilu" with a shaddah. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it without a shaddah. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "bi-ayyati ardin," and the rest read "bi-ayyi ardin." Al-Farra' said: He was content with the feminine of "ard" (land) rather than the feminine of "ayy." It was also said: By "ard" he meant "makan" (place), so he used the masculine. The poet said:

"Neither a cloud has poured its pouring, nor a land has made its herbage sprout as it sprouted."

[[The speaker is Amir ibn Juwayn al-Ta'i. He describes a fertile land because of how much rain fell upon it. Al-muzna: the cloud. Al-wadq: the rain.]]

Al-Akhfash said: It is permissible to say "marartu bi-jariyatin ayyi jariyatin" and "ayyati jariyatin." Sibawayh compared the feminine of "ayy" to the feminine of "kull" in their saying: "kullatuhunna."

(Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.) "Khabir" is either an adjective of "'Alim" or a second predicate. And Allah knows best.
